short: An attempt to knock the Ottomans out of the war that cost half a million casualties.
full:
After a naval attempt to force the Dardanelles failed in March 1915 with three battleships sunk by mines, the Allies put troops ashore on the Gallipoli peninsula on 25 April. British and French divisions landed at Cape Helles; the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps came ashore further north at a cove backed by steep, scrub-covered ridges. Ottoman defenders, among them Mustafa Kemal, held the high ground, and the beachheads never became more than shallow footholds.

Eight months of stalemate followed, with heat, flies, dysentery and a fresh failure at Suvla Bay in August. The evacuation, completed on 9 January 1916, was the one unqualified success of the campaign: the beaches were cleared without a single casualty. Around 56,000 Ottoman and 44,000 Allied troops died. Churchill, who had pressed the operation as First Lord of the Admiralty, left the government over it. The landing became a founding national memory in Australia and New Zealand, and made the reputation of the future Ataturk.
